summary: Explains how TRILL, a protocol that uses IS-IS to forward traffic across multi-hop networks, handles LANs with several RBridges. It describes appointing forwarders so one RBridge handles each VLAN's traffic. It updates RFC 6325, and was replaced by RFC 8139.

plainLanguage.summary:
Several TRILL switches can be attached to the same network link. RFC 6439 explains how those switches arrange for only one of them to handle the traffic of each VLAN on that link, so that frames cannot loop.

One switch, the Designated RBridge, sends the list of which switch handles which VLANs. Every switch also keeps timers that hold it back for a while when it hears that another switch has taken over a VLAN.

questions: what is an appointed forwarder in trill
how does the trill designated rbridge appoint forwarders
subtitle: How TRILL decides which of several switches on one link handles the traffic of each VLAN.

tldr.problem: When several RBridges are attached to the same link, more than one of them could handle native frames for the same VLAN, and the resulting loop is not covered by the TRILL hop count.
tldr.mechanism: The Designated RBridge appoints other RBridges as Appointed Forwarders for ranges of VLANs, using sub-TLVs inside its TRILL Hellos. Each RBridge also keeps inhibition timers that stop it forwarding native frames for a VLAN while another RBridge may already be handling that VLAN.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6439 documents that mechanism in detail and updates RFC 6325. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 8139.

today: RFC 6439 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8139 and updated by RFC 7180. It updated RFC 6325, so RFC 8139 is the text to read for the Appointed Forwarder mechanism today.

sections.title: Appointed Forwarders on a Shared Link
sections.content:
TRILL is a protocol that forwards data frames across a network with many hops and an arbitrary topology. It uses IS-IS link state routing to work out paths, and it wraps each frame in a header that carries a hop count. Devices that implement TRILL are called RBridges.

TRILL supports multi-access links, where several end stations and several RBridges are attached to the same link. When more than one RBridge is attached, the native traffic to and from the end stations on that link is handled by a subset of those RBridges called Appointed Forwarders. The intent is that the native traffic in each VLAN (Virtual LAN) is handled by at most one RBridge. One RBridge can be the Appointed Forwarder for many VLANs.

The purpose of this document is to improve the documentation of the Appointed Forwarder mechanism, so it updates RFC 6325. It includes reference implementation details, but other implementations that interoperate on the wire are permitted. Where the two documents conflict, RFC 6439 prevails.

The mechanism does not apply to a link where no end station service is offered, such as a point-to-point IS-IS link or a link where every RBridge port is a trunk port. It has no effect on adjacency formation, on the election of the Designated RBridge, on MTU matching or on pseudonode formation. It only affects the handling of native frames; it has no effect on the forwarding of TRILL Data frames.
sections.plainLanguage: Several TRILL switches can sit on the same network link. This RFC sets out how they arrange for only one switch to handle the traffic of each VLAN on that link, which stops frames from looping.

sections.title: Who the Appointed Forwarder Is
sections.content:
The Appointed Forwarder on a link for VLAN-x is the RBridge that takes native frames in from the link and sends native frames out to the link in VLAN-x. By default the Designated RBridge (DRB) on a link is in charge of native traffic for all VLANs on that link. The DRB may act as Appointed Forwarder for any VLAN itself, and it may appoint other RBridges that have ports on the link.

It matters that there are not two Appointed Forwarders on a link taking and sending native frames for the same VLAN at the same time. If there were, they could form a loop in which frames are not protected by a TRILL hop count. The same can happen with two Appointed Forwarders for two different VLANs, VLAN-x and VLAN-y, if ports or bridges inside the link are configured to map frames between those VLANs.

There are three ways an RBridge can be appointed or un-appointed: a change in the DRB election, action by the DRB, and a local configuration change. An RBridge that believes it has become the DRB can act as Appointed Forwarder for any VLANs on the link that it chooses, as long as its port is not configured as a trunk port and has that VLAN enabled. It loses all Appointed Forwarder status when it decides it has lost DRB status, or when it observes a change in the DRB without itself becoming the DRB.

Disabling a VLAN at an RBridge port cancels that RBridge's Appointed Forwarder status for the VLAN, unless the VLAN is enabled on another port of the same RBridge on the same link. Configuring a port as a trunk port or a point-to-point port revokes any status that depended on enabled VLANs at that port. Enabling a VLAN again does not by itself make the RBridge an Appointed Forwarder.
sections.plainLanguage:
For a given link and a given VLAN, one RBridge is in charge of the frames coming from and going to the end stations attached there. That RBridge is the Appointed Forwarder for that VLAN.

Two RBridges in charge at the same time could pass frames back and forth, and the TRILL hop count does not stop that. The RFC therefore adds timers that hold a switch back while a change is in progress.

sections.title: How the DRB Appoints and Removes Forwarders
sections.content:
The DRB appoints other RBridges by including one or more Appointed Forwarders sub-TLVs in a TRILL Hello that it sends on the Designated VLAN out the port that won the DRB election. When the DRB sends any appointments in a TRILL Hello, it must send all appointments for that link in that Hello. Any previous appointment not included is implicitly revoked. The DRB MUST NOT send any appointments on a link unless its DRB inhibition timer for that link has expired.

A non-DRB RBridge that can offer end station service on a link checks the source MAC address, the Port ID and the System ID in the Hello to find out whether it came from the winning DRB port. If it did not, any Appointed Forwarder sub-TLVs in the Hello are ignored and its status does not change. If no Appointed Forwarder sub-TLVs are present, its status does not change either.

If the Hello is from the winning DRB port and carries one or more Appointed Forwarder sub-TLVs, the receiving RBridge becomes appointed for the VLANs that are both listed for it in the Hello and enabled on the receiving port. VLAN IDs 0x000 and 0xFFF are ignored. It loses Appointed Forwarder status for any other VLAN it was forwarding.

An appointment covers one RBridge and a contiguous interval of VLAN IDs, and it appoints that RBridge only for the VLANs in that interval that are enabled on one or more of its ports on the link. For scattered sets, such as every even-numbered VLAN, the network manager can enable only those VLANs on the target port and have the DRB appoint the RBridge for all VLANs. Because the Designated VLAN should be enabled on every RBridge port on the link, the general case needs two appointments: the example in the RFC appoints an RBridge for all VLANs from 1 through 100 and from 102 through 4,094 when the Designated VLAN is 101.

The DRB need not repeat appointments in every Hello, but it is RECOMMENDED that it send them on the Designated VLAN at least once per its Holding Time on the port that won the election. The RFC estimates that appointments for 83 RBridges fit in under 1000 bytes of a Hello, and says that more than 65 Appointed Forwarders on a link is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage:
The DRB sends the list of appointments inside a Hello, the same kind of message RBridges use to say hello on a link. A Hello that arrives from any other port is ignored, so only the DRB's own port can hand out this work.

Each appointment covers a block of consecutive VLAN numbers. To spread the work over scattered VLAN numbers, the network manager enables only those VLANs on the port that will do the work, and the appointment covers everything else too.

sections.title: The Inhibition Timers
sections.content:
An RBridge keeps, for every link on which it can offer end station service, a DRB inhibition timer, a root change inhibition timer and up to 4,094 VLAN inhibition timers, one for each legal VLAN ID. The DRB and root change timers MUST be implemented. At least two VLAN timers MUST be implemented, and they may be merged with care. An RBridge MUST NOT merge the timers of two VLANs if it is the Appointed Forwarder for one of them and not the other, because that can prolong inhibition indefinitely.

The timers are set by eight rules. On boot or management reset, each port has its own set of timers, all expired except the DRB inhibition timer. Becoming the DRB sets the DRB inhibition timer to the Holding Time of the port that won the election; losing DRB status sets it to expired. When an RBridge receives a Hello saying that the sender is the Appointed Forwarder for VLAN-x, it sets its VLAN-x timer to the larger of its current value and the Holding Time in that Hello. Enabling a VLAN on a link for the first time sets that VLAN's timer to the port's Holding Time.

On detecting a change in the common spanning tree root bridge on a port, the RBridge sets the root change timer to a time that defaults to 30 seconds and is configurable from 30 down to zero. The RFC suggests 7 seconds if Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol runs throughout the attached bridged LAN, or 4 seconds if the attached bridges have a minimum Bridge Hello Timer. When two ports are found to be on the same link, their timers merge by taking the maximum; when they are found to be on separate links, the timers are cloned.
sections.plainLanguage:
Each RBridge runs timers on every link where it can serve end stations. A timer that has not run out means the RBridge must not forward native frames for that VLAN yet, because another RBridge may already be doing it.

The timers are set by fixed rules. The DRB timer is set when an RBridge wins the DRB election, the VLAN timer is pushed out whenever a Hello says somebody else is handling that VLAN, and the root change timer is set when the spanning tree root moves.

sections.title: What an Inhibited Forwarder Does
sections.content:
An Appointed Forwarder is inhibited for VLAN-x if its DRB inhibition timer, its root change inhibition timer or its VLAN-x inhibition timer has not expired. An inhibited forwarder still decapsulates a TRILL Data frame for VLAN-x, but it does not output it or queue it for that link, although it may do so for other links. A native frame received in VLAN-x from that link is ignored, except for address learning.

An RBridge with unexpired inhibition timers is still required to say in the Hellos it sends on VLAN-x whether it is the Appointed Forwarder for VLAN-x on the port where it sends the Hello. Inhibition has no effect on the receipt or forwarding of TRILL Data frames.

An RBridge may have several ports on the same link. Ports suspended because of a duplicate MAC address never ingress or egress native frames. If the RBridge is the forwarder for a VLAN across several non-suspended ports, it may share the load between them as it chooses, as long as a frame sent out of one port cannot come back in on another of its ports.

TRILL Hellos carry the VLAN in which they were sent. If a Hello sent on VLAN-y arrives on VLAN-x, VLAN mapping is happening inside the link. To prevent a loop from that mapping, the DRB MUST make or revoke appointments so that the same RBridge is the Appointed Forwarder for both VLAN-x and VLAN-y.
sections.plainLanguage: An RBridge whose timer has not run out still reads and unwraps frames, but it does not put native frames onto that link and it ignores native frames arriving from the link. It keeps telling the other RBridges in its Hellos what role it holds.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: RFC 6439 provides improved documentation of the TRILL Appointed Forwarder mechanism. It does not change the security considerations of the TRILL base protocol, and it points readers to Section 6 of RFC 6325.
sections.plainLanguage: This document only explains the Appointed Forwarder rules more clearly. It adds no security rules of its own and points to the base TRILL document for those.

items.title: DRB inhibition timer
items.text: Set to the Holding Time of the winning port when an RBridge becomes the DRB, and set to expired when it loses DRB status.

items.title: Root change inhibition timer
items.text: Set when the common spanning tree root changes. It defaults to 30 seconds and is configurable from 30 down to zero.

items.title: VLAN inhibition timer
items.text: One per legal VLAN ID, up to 4,094 of them. Extended whenever a Hello says another RBridge is the Appointed Forwarder for that VLAN.
